tasks.prompt:
Build a small multi-user chat in the current working directory: a Python
backend on aiohttp, a plain JavaScript frontend, and an automated test for
it. A checker will start your server, talk to it over WebSocket, and drive
the page in a headless browser like a real user (typing and clicking).
Follow the contract below exactly.

## Files

- `server.py`
- `static/index.html`
- `static/app.js`
- `static/style.css`
- `test_chat.py`

## Server (`server.py`)

- Python 3 with aiohttp. It is started as `python3 server.py` from the
  working directory and must keep running until it is killed.
- Port: the `PORT` environment variable, default `8765`. Listen on `0.0.0.0`
  or `127.0.0.1`: the checker connects to `127.0.0.1`.
- `GET /` returns `static/index.html`. Every file in `static/` is also served
  at `/static/<name>`, and `index.html` loads `/static/style.css` and
  `/static/app.js` from there.
- The WebSocket endpoint is `/ws` on the same port.

## Protocol

Every WebSocket message is a text frame holding one JSON object.

Client to server:

- `{"type": "join", "nick": "<nick>"}`
- `{"type": "message", "text": "<text>"}`

Server to client:

- `{"type": "history", "messages": [...]}`: sent only to the client that
  joined, right after its `join`. `messages` holds the last 50 chat messages,
  oldest first, each in the `message` form below. System notices are not
  part of the history.
- `{"type": "system", "text": "..."}`: sent to every joined client when a
  client joins and when a joined client leaves (its WebSocket closes). The
  text names the nick, e.g. `alice joined`, `alice left`. Whether the joining
  client also receives its own join notice is up to you.
- `{"type": "message", "nick": "...", "text": "...", "ts": <number>}`: when a
  joined client sends a message, the server broadcasts it to every joined
  client, the sender included. `nick` is the sender's nick, `ts` is the
  server time in Unix milliseconds.

A client that is connected but has not joined gets no broadcasts, and its
`message` frames are ignored.

## Page

- `static/index.html` has elements with exactly these ids: `nick` (text
  input), `join-btn` (button), `msg` (text input), `send-btn` (button),
  `messages` (the chat feed).
- No auto-join. Loading the page must never send `join` by itself, not even
  with a default or remembered nick: the user joins only by acting. Until
  then `#nick` and `#join-btn` are visible and enabled, and `#messages` is
  empty (no placeholder text).
- Clicking `#join-btn` joins with the nick typed into `#nick`. Pressing Enter
  in `#nick` does the same.
- After joining, `#msg` and `#send-btn` are visible and enabled (before
  joining they may be hidden or disabled). Pressing Enter in `#msg` or
  clicking `#send-btn` sends the typed text as a message.
- On join, `#messages` shows the received history. After that, every
  incoming `message` and `system` notice is appended to `#messages` with its
  text visible. A message is shown when its broadcast comes back from the
  server (the sender receives its own broadcast too).
- The page may open the WebSocket on load or when the user joins.
- Plain JavaScript: no frameworks, no build step, nothing loaded from the
  internet. The checker's browser can reach only your server.

## Test (`test_chat.py`)

Write your own automated test and ship it with the code:

- It runs as `python3 test_chat.py` from the working directory, needs
  nothing already running, and finishes within 60 seconds.
- It starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess (use `sys.executable`), with
  `PORT` set to a free port it picks, waits until the server accepts
  connections, and stops the server at the end, also when a check fails.
- It checks the protocol with real WebSocket clients: join and history,
  broadcast between two clients, join and leave notices, history for a
  newcomer.
- It exits with status 0 only if every check passed, non-zero otherwise.

## Environment

`python3` on your PATH has aiohttp available. It is the same Python the
checker uses to run `server.py` and `test_chat.py`, so there is nothing to
install. Do not install packages globally. You may start the server and run
your test while you work, but you don't have to. Stop any server you started
before you finish.

Build a small kanban board web app in the current directory: an aiohttp backend `server.py`, started as `python3 server.py`, that listens on the port from the `PORT` environment variable (default 8770) and serves the page at `/`, and a plain JavaScript frontend with no frameworks, no build step and nothing loaded from the internet. The board has three columns, To Do, Doing and Done, behind a JSON API: `GET /api/cards` returns the list of all cards, each an object `{"id": ..., "title": ..., "column": ...}` with a unique id and the column `todo`, `doing` or `done`; `POST /api/cards` with `{"title": ...}` creates a card in `todo` and returns it, or answers 400 when the title is blank; `PATCH /api/cards/<id>` with `{"column": ...}` moves the card and returns it, or answers 400 for an unknown column; `DELETE /api/cards/<id>` removes the card; and both of the last two answer 404 for an id that does not exist. Every change is saved, before the server answers, to a JSON file at the path from the `BOARD_FILE` environment variable (default `board.json`; no file yet means an empty board), so the board survives a restart of the server, even a hard kill. The page has a text input `#new-card` and a button `#add-btn` that adds a card with the typed title (pressing Enter in the input does the same), and column elements `#todo`, `#doing` and `#done` that hold one `.card` element per card, showing its title, with the buttons `.move-left` and `.move-right` to move it to the neighbouring column (they may be missing or disabled where there is none) and `.delete`; the page changes the board only through the API, loads it when it opens and always shows it exactly as the server stores it. Write `test_board.py`, an automated test that starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess on a free port with its own temporary `BOARD_FILE`, checks the API, stops the server even when a check fails, finishes within 60 seconds and exits 0 only if everything works, then run it and make it pass. `python3` on your PATH already has aiohttp, so install nothing, and stop the servers you started before you finish, each by the PID of the process you launched — never by matching names with pkill or killall: other processes on this machine are not yours.

# Kanban board web app

## Brief

Build a small kanban board web app in the current directory: an aiohttp
backend, a plain JavaScript page and an automated test. The board has three
columns, To Do, Doing and Done; cards can be added, moved between columns and
deleted, and the board is kept in a JSON file, so it survives a restart.

## Requirements

### Server

- `server.py`, on aiohttp, started as `python3 server.py`.
- Port: the `PORT` environment variable, default `8770`.
- Serves the page at `/`.

### JSON API

- `GET /api/cards` returns the list of all cards. A card is an object
  `{"id": ..., "title": ..., "column": ...}`: the id is unique, the column is
  `todo`, `doing` or `done`.
- `POST /api/cards` with `{"title": ...}` creates a card in `todo` and returns
  it. A blank title: 400.
- `PATCH /api/cards/<id>` with `{"column": ...}` moves the card and returns it.
  An unknown column: 400.
- `DELETE /api/cards/<id>` removes the card.
- `PATCH` and `DELETE` answer 404 for an id that does not exist.

### Storage

- Every change is saved, before the server answers, to a JSON file at the
  path from the `BOARD_FILE` environment variable, default `board.json`.
- No file yet means an empty board.
- The board survives a restart of the server, even a hard kill.

### Page

- Plain JavaScript: no frameworks, no build step, nothing loaded from the
  internet.
- A text input `#new-card` and a button `#add-btn` that adds a card with the
  typed title. Pressing Enter in the input does the same.
- Column elements `#todo`, `#doing` and `#done`, holding one `.card` element
  per card.
- Each `.card` shows its title and has the buttons `.move-left` and
  `.move-right` (move it to the neighbouring column; they may be missing or
  disabled where there is none) and `.delete`.
- The page changes the board only through the API, loads it when it opens and
  always shows it exactly as the server stores it.

### Test: `test_board.py`

- Starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess on a free port with its own
  temporary `BOARD_FILE`.
- Checks the API.
- Stops the server, even when a check fails.
- Finishes within 60 seconds and exits 0 only if everything works.
- You run it and make it pass.

### Environment

- `python3` on your PATH already has aiohttp: install nothing.
- Stop the servers you started before you finish, each by the PID of the
  process you launched — never by matching names with pkill or killall: other
  processes on this machine are not yours.

## Plan

Work in this order and finish each step before the next.

1. **Server and storage.** Write `server.py`: the port, the board loaded from
   `BOARD_FILE`, the four API routes with their 400 and 404 answers, a save on
   every change.
2. **Check the API by hand.** Start the server with a temporary `BOARD_FILE`
   and walk the API: create, a blank title, move, an unknown column, delete,
   an unknown id. Kill the server with SIGKILL, start it again on the same
   `BOARD_FILE` and confirm that the board is unchanged.
3. **Page.** Serve it at `/` with the required ids and classes. It loads the
   board when it opens; adding (button and Enter), moving left and right and
   deleting go through the API; after every action the page shows the board as
   the server stores it.
4. **Test.** Write `test_board.py` as required above.
5. **Run and fix.** Run `python3 test_board.py` until it passes, then go
   through the Definition of Done item by item and fix what fails.
6. **Clean up.** Stop every server you started.

## TODO

- [ ] `server.py` starts with `python3 server.py`, port from `PORT` (default 8770)
- [ ] `GET /` serves the page
- [ ] `GET /api/cards`
- [ ] `POST /api/cards`, 400 for a blank title
- [ ] `PATCH /api/cards/<id>`, 400 for an unknown column, 404 for an unknown id
- [ ] `DELETE /api/cards/<id>`, 404 for an unknown id
- [ ] Board saved to `BOARD_FILE` on every change, before answering; loaded at start; no file means an empty board
- [ ] Page: `#new-card` and `#add-btn`, Enter adds too
- [ ] Page: `#todo`, `#doing`, `#done` with one `.card` per card: title, `.move-left`, `.move-right`, `.delete`
- [ ] Page: loads the board on open, changes it only through the API, always shows it as the server stores it
- [ ] `test_board.py` written, run, passing
- [ ] Every Definition of Done item checked
- [ ] Every server you started is stopped

## Definition of Done

The task is done when all of the following hold.

API and storage, with the server started on a `BOARD_FILE` that does not exist yet:

1. `GET /` answers 200 with the page; `GET /api/cards` answers 200 with `[]`.
2. `POST /api/cards` with a title answers 2xx with the new card: an id, the
   same title, the column `todo`. Three cards get three different ids, and
   `GET /api/cards` lists all three in `todo`.
3. `POST /api/cards` with the title `""` or `"   "` answers 400 and creates
   nothing.
4. `PATCH /api/cards/<id>` to any of the three columns answers 2xx with the
   card in that column, and `GET /api/cards` agrees. With
   `{"column": "archive"}` it answers 400 and the card stays where it was.
5. `DELETE /api/cards/<id>` answers 2xx, and the card is gone from
   `GET /api/cards`.
6. `PATCH` and `DELETE` of an id that does not exist, or no longer exists,
   answer 404.
7. After a change the file at `BOARD_FILE` exists and holds valid JSON.
8. Killed with SIGKILL right after a change and started again on the same
   `BOARD_FILE`, the server returns exactly the same cards: ids, titles,
   columns. A card created after the restart gets an id no other card has, and
   it survives the next SIGKILL and restart as well.

Page, in a real browser, typing and clicking like a user:

9. Cards that are already stored show up when the page opens, each as one
   `.card` in its column (`#todo`, `#doing`, `#done`).
10. Typing a title into `#new-card` and pressing Enter adds the card to
    `#todo`, on the page and on the server. Typing a title and clicking
    `#add-btn` does the same.
11. Clicking `#add-btn` with an empty or blank title adds nothing, neither on
    the page nor on the server.
12. `.move-right` on a card in `#todo` moves it to `#doing`, once more to
    `#done`; `.move-left` on it in `#done` moves it back to `#doing`. After
    each click the card is in exactly one column on the page, and the server
    has it in the same column.
13. `.delete` removes the card from the page and from the server.
14. The page never shows more or fewer cards than the server has. Reloading
    it, or opening it in a second browser, shows the same board.

Test:

15. `python3 test_board.py`, with nothing running beforehand, exits 0 within
    60 seconds and leaves no server running.
16. If `server.py` cannot start (say, it exits at once), `python3 test_board.py`
    exits non-zero.

# Multi-user WebSocket chat

## Brief

Build a small multi-user chat in the current working directory: a Python
backend on aiohttp, a plain JavaScript frontend and an automated test. Users
open the page, join under the nick they type and exchange messages over a
WebSocket; a newcomer sees the recent history. A checker will start your
server, talk to it over WebSocket, and drive the page in a headless browser
like a real user (typing and clicking). Follow the requirements below exactly.

- `static/index.html`
- `static/app.js`
- `static/style.css`
- `test_chat.py`

- The WebSocket endpoint is `/ws` on the same port.

A client that is connected but has not joined gets no broadcasts, and its

- `static/index.html` has elements with exactly these ids: `nick` (text

- It runs as `python3 test_chat.py` from the working directory, needs nothing

- It starts `server.py` itself as a subprocess (use `sys.executable`), with

The task is done when all of the following hold.

Protocol, with the server started as `python3 server.py` and `PORT` set to a
free port:

2. The server answers HTTP on `127.0.0.1` at that port and keeps running.
3. A client that opens a WebSocket at `/ws` and sends `join` receives a

   and a `ts` that is a positive number.

   receive a `system` notice that names its nick.

   messages sent so far, oldest first, each with its `nick`, `text` and `ts`,
   and no system notices.

   one of them is broadcast, and a newcomer's `history` holds exactly the last
   50, oldest first.

    editable, `#join-btn` is visible and enabled.

12. Typing a text into `#msg` and pressing Enter sends it: every joined client

    page's own `#messages`.
13. Typing a text into `#msg` and clicking `#send-btn` does the same.
14. On a second page, typing a nick into `#nick` and clicking `#join-btn`
    joins: its `#messages` shows the texts of the messages sent before, and
    the first page's `#messages` shows a notice that names the newcomer.
15. A message sent from the second page appears in the first page's
    `#messages`.

16. `python3 test_chat.py`, with nothing running beforehand, exits 0 within 60
